subject: Advanced Science
central_question: How do valence electrons explain simple covalent structures, exceptions to the octet rule, and the characteristic properties of metals?
in_scope_units: Incomplete octets with lithium, beryllium, boron, and BF3
Quick Check on octet rule and its exceptions
Metallic bonding as attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
Electron sea model and electrical conductivity
Check Your Understanding and assertion-reason questions on metallic bonding
banned_topics: Hydrogen spectra, Rutherford model, and Bohr model questions carried over from the preceding chapter
VSEPR molecular shapes and bond angles

known_pitfalls.claim: The octet rule is an absolute law that every stable molecule must obey.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter explicitly describes it as a useful guiding principle with stable exceptions such as BF3, SF6, and NO.

known_pitfalls.claim: Hydrogen must have eight electrons around it to be stable.
known_pitfalls.correction: Hydrogen follows a duplet arrangement and attains two electrons like helium.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every dot in a Lewis structure represents a bonding electron.
known_pitfalls.correction: Only the shared pair between bonded atoms is a bonding pair; the remaining dots are non-bonding electrons or lone pairs.

known_pitfalls.claim: Boron in BF3 is unstable because it has only six electrons around it.
known_pitfalls.correction: BF3 is a stable incomplete-octet exception in which boron forms three bonds and has six electrons around the central atom.

known_pitfalls.claim: SF6 follows the ordinary octet rule because sulfur has eight electrons.
known_pitfalls.correction: Sulfur is surrounded by twelve bonding electrons in SF6, so it is an expanded-octet exception.

known_pitfalls.claim: NO can give every atom a complete octet despite having eleven valence electrons.
known_pitfalls.correction: An odd total number of electrons means at least one electron remains unpaired and at least one atom has an incomplete octet.

known_pitfalls.claim: Metallic bonding occurs because valence electrons are completely transferred to individual metal ions.
known_pitfalls.correction: In the electron sea model, outer electrons are delocalised and shared collectively throughout the metal.

known_pitfalls.claim: Metallic bonds are localised between fixed pairs of atoms like covalent bonds.
known_pitfalls.correction: Metallic bonding is non-directional because mobile electrons attract many positive ions collectively.

recommended_example_progression: Use the fluorine Lewis symbol and the hydrogen fluoride example in Section 7.1.1 to distinguish bonding and non-bonding electrons.
Use Quick Check 7 to draw BF3 and explain boron’s six-electron incomplete octet.
Use Quick Check 8 to analyse why SF6 is an expanded-octet exception.
Use Quick Check 6 to explain why NO is an odd-electron exception.
Use Fig. 7.1 to identify fixed positive metal ions and a mobile sea of electrons.
Use Fig. 7.2 and Check Your Understanding Q6 to explain electrical conduction.
Use Check Your Understanding Q8, Q9, Q13, and assertion-reason Q21 to connect non-directional metallic bonding with malleability and ductility.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter contains a 'Quick Check' after octet-rule exceptions and a 'Check Your Understanding' section with conceptual and assertion-reason questions on metallic bonding.

beyond_the_textbook: Lewis structures are useful bookkeeping models for valence electrons, but they do not by themselves show the exact three-dimensional shape of a molecule.
Odd-electron species such as NO are often called radicals and can be especially reactive because of their unpaired electron.
The simple electron sea model explains many metallic properties, while more advanced solid-state physics uses energy bands to describe electrons in metals.
Alloys remain metallic but can have different hardness, strength, and conductivity because atoms of different sizes disturb the regular ion arrangement.
Metallic conductivity usually changes with temperature because electron motion is affected by increased vibration of the ion lattice.
